All images © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta. Sanlé Sory photographed at Volta Photo Studio in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso.

The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography

When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”

“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough. 

Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world.

“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator

Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West. 

But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says. 

She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves. 

The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”

Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator.  

Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African. 

Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted.

“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery,  London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour

items.title_es: La obra de color de Sanlé Sory viene a la galería de fotógrafos
items.content_es:
Todas las imágenes © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Cortesía de Tezeta. Sanlé Sory fotografiado en Volta Photo Studio en Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso.

La obra posterior del artista de Burkina Faso revela los cambios ethos y cambios sociopolíticos en la fotografía de África Occidental

Cuando se le pregunta por qué la Galería de Fotógrafos muestra obras de color más adelante del fotógrafo de estudio de Burkina Faso Sanlé Sory – y por qué ahora – la respuesta del comisario Taous Dahmani es clara y directa: “Porque estoy aquí ahora”.

“Siempre había querido pensar en la larga tradición de la fotografía del estudio de África Occidental como una superficie global”, añade. Alimentado con lecturas dominantes, Dahmani argumenta que estas fotografías requieren una reubicación de la función si deben ser comprendidas de maneras más generativas y restaurativas. El trabajo del fotógrafo es un paisaje político, artístico, a menudo polémico y gestural; es también, fundamentalmente, un trabajo.

Tal vez el “arte fino” – lo que eso significa – es un cáliz penetrado, un pedestal trapdoorado, una jaula dorada. En cambio, Sory está aquí un artesano maestro, pero uno que busca ser pagado en lugar de interrumpir el canon. Esta maldición del arte fino, que fija la obra y el carácter de Sory en algo descubierto, exige recontextualización, y posterior elevación, a su mundo cierra una vez.

“[La obra de color posterior de Sory] tiene un cambio bastante significativo en lo que sabemos de la historia de la práctica africana occidental” – Taous Dahmani, curador

Las lecturas reductivas a menudo colocan este tipo de fotógrafo, y por extensión fotografía, como un acontecimiento histórico sobre un ser viviente. Dahmani dados que esta lectura limitada "refugia la entrada en la contemporalidad", y perpetua las narraciones del arte occidental como "formas aceptables de nostalgia sobre este pasado de liberación, una llamada al tiempo "cuando liberamos a los pobres africanos" .

Pero el archivo de Sory tiene “miles y millas” de negativos de colores posteriores, muchos de los cuales nunca han sido impresos más allá de su comisión original. Dahmani pregunta por qué y dirige hacia una reubicación, una “re-anclaje” en sus. Tal vez estos colores funciona, un movimiento de la anterior obra de blanco y negro de los años 60 y 70, se consideró más difícil de digerir para los términos públicos algo menos menos

Ella lee la práctica como omnipresente y única; más cerca de las historias funcionales, políticas y sociales atrapadas dentro de los retratos, y entendidas como artefactos totalmente comisionados. Sin embargo, al comisariar el espectáculo en Londres hay una conciencia de que el hogar no siempre es un lugar al que se puede volver, que tal vez no hay verdadera providencia contextual. En lugar de eso hay una posibilidad de ser nuevas tierras, formas de ellas permiten

La lectura del arte occidental tiene una tendencia a convertir a las naciones africanas en islas, deslocalizarlas de historias vecinas y concurrentes. Dahmani se refiere a esto como una “historia condenada y fetichizada”, uno que el mercado abraza con facilidad pero que no nos acerca a entender estas imágenes o personas. “Para mí, el color se convirtió en el punto de partida”, dice. “Podemos pensar críticamente sobre esta historia a color?

Los retratos posteriores de Sory de vender ambulantes, personal y directo, se extendieron por un lento apetito por retratos comisionados. Los camarógrafos habían llegado y los tiempos estaban cambiando. Dahmani también destaca los deseos de los tarados que se le encargó grabar, comentando sobre su entrada en las imágenes. “Sory impreso en blanco y negro, pero cuando el color se hizo más accesible, los clientes le preguntaron.

Dahmani traza historias de los sitters a través de reubicaciones históricas; cada vez que notan a alguien vestido fanciosamente para la cámara, que está "desgastando un trayecto demasiado pequeño, sus zapatos tal vez desenterrados". A través de estas imágenes Dahmani se aleja de una lectura de moda hacia algo más parece a los estudios de estilo socialmente informado, un análisis de recaídas de mano y falsificado.

Sory tuvo que negociar y barrer con sus súbditos, ya que en última instancia las imágenes existían fuera de sus pagos. Tenía que seguir las tendencias, mantenerse al día con los tiempos cambiantes. De arrepentido la gente no quería que sus famosos fondos ilustrados más tiempo. “Querían ser parte de una nueva tecnología, y una nueva capacidad de ser visto,” explica Dahmani. Sory, como con muchos retratistas de África Occidental

“Ahora no tengo que probar la fotografía es una forma de arte”, afirma Dahmani. “Pero sí quiero volver al hecho de que en realidad, históricamente, había cosas que eramos demasiado rápidos para poner en una categoría, en lugar de permitirles ser una multiplicidad de cosas. Y no creo que a menudo permitimos que los artistas africanos fueran una multiplicidad de cosas.”

items.content:
Abdus Subhan and Fathema Begum. From Londoni Memoirs © Seema Khalique

Realising that the experiences of a whole generation of British-Bangladeshis will soon be lost – and motivated by celebrating the community in the midst of a rising far right – Seema Khalique built a multi-faceted piece of history now on show in London’s Bethnal Green

Seema Khalique’s father Abdul arrived in the UK from Bangladesh in 1956; her mother, Gulnehar, arrived in 1973, after the Bangladesh Liberation War. Abdul Khalique was in the restaurant business, and the family moved to Croydon in the 1970s after buying a restaurant there; later they moved to Eltham, once again following work. It’s a story that speaks of graft and determination, the sheer grit required to start a new life in a new country. But there are also gaps in the narrative. As Khalique’s father grew older, she realised she knew little about his early London years, or what it had been like to arrive in the UK. She realised that he and a whole generation of British Bangladeshis would soon pass away, and with them these experiences would be lost. 

And so connecting with 12 individuals – many linked to her father – Khalique spent hours with each of them from 2021 on, listening to their stories, collaborating on their portraits, and looking through their archives. The result is Londoni Memoirs, a still on-going project supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, which gathers oral history, archive photos, ephemera, and new images to document Bangaldeshis who settled in Britain in the 1950s-70s. Some, like Khalique, are based in London, others are further afield, landing by luck and the work that was available when they migrated. 

“Generally all the participants moved where there was work, so if that meant going to Birmingham, because of the factory trade there, they were in Birmingham,” says Khalique. “There was a massive community in the East End because of the factories there, and that created opportunities for women working from home – they could do sewing and tailoring, and be with the kids. Everyone had a sewing machine. Most people worked six days a week. One of the participants lived in St Albans and his general pattern, when he worked, was to work from four in the morning until four in the afternoon at a factory, then the evening shift at a restaurant.”

By working at this level people managed to set themselves up, says Khalique; many were also sending money to Bangladesh, particularly during the war [in 1971]. “Many people spoke about feeling that they had helped Bangladesh survive,” she says. “Family members didn’t starve because they were able to provide.”

Londoni Memoirs collects some heartbreaking stories, tales of people fleeing burning villages – the only ones to escape – and returning years later, not knowing who they would find alive. Few of the participants had spoken publicly about these experiences before, says Khalique, preferring to move on “though they still carry the trauma”. But Londoni Memoirs also records happier times, Khalique determined not to flatten a range of experiences into a monotone, or many testimonies into a single lumpen mass. 

“One participant came from a very affluent family, he came to the UK to study law and his father basically funded him,” she points out. “He lived on the same road as The Beatles, and had these crazy stories about parties where the police would chase everyone away. Others spoke about squatting in London, as a solution to the housing crisis. It was interesting to hear about the parallel lives that were lived at that time, and to hear about not just the struggles that we associate with migration, but the enjoyment that comes from it. Experiencing cold weather, snowball fights, all of it.” 

Khalique’s sensitivity shows in her portraits, which she made collaboratively. There’s a sweet photograph of her mother in her garden, wearing a green sari matching the foliage of a Bangladeshi Marrow Plant “which the Bangladeshi grow with pride in the summer months”. Some of the women preferred not to be shown looking straight at the camera though, wary of the sin of idolatry; Khalique has also collected other images, which present other images and do other things. There’s a formal studio portrait of Rajia Yaqub and family, for example, a snap of Makhlisur Rahman standing with his house and a smart car; often taken to send back home, these shots present carefully-constructed images of happiness and prosperity, not everyday trials or tribulations.

Khalique has also collected passport photos and official documentation, including an amazingly glamorous photograph of her mother in a passport due to expire in 1977, and a receipt from the Pakistan Relief Fund for £5, dated in pre-independence 1965 [when £5 was worth about £125 today]. Khalique’s exhibition at Four Corners includes 10-minute videos of the participants speaking; she’s also created transcripts of the videos, and published them in a newspaper. “I know not everyone will sit and watch all the videos,” she says. “So the newspaper was important, and then it can also travel.”

The location of the gallery is important too because, though Khalique still lives in South East London, she wanted to show the work somewhere close to the British-Bangladeshi community; Four Corners is in East London, near the long-standing Banglatown in Whitechapel and Brick Lane. Few of the participants could come to the opening night, as they’re now elderly and some in poor health, but ten were able to come for a special afternoon, and for Khalique that was deeply rewarding. They were wowed by seeing their portraits and archive photographs on the walls, she says, adding she had framed these images to ensure they felt properly honoured. 

Khalique also arranged a family workshop in the gallery, allowing children to find out more about British, Bangladeshi, and British-Bangladeshi history, plus issues of representation; these issues have become more important to her, she says, because of hardening far right attitudes, and because she now has kids of her own. “I grew up in a very multicultural area, growing up I never felt racially different,” she says. “It’s only since becoming a mother I’ve realised that, and only in the last few years I’ve experienced it. And that pains me because, while I can fight for myself, my children can’t fight for themselves. So I felt I had to do it for them. I wanted to make work that would celebrate this community.”

Londoni Memoirs by Seema Khalique is on show at Four Corners until 10 October www.fourcornersfilm.co.uk www.seemakhalique.com

items.title_es: Reunir las memorias de Londres y la experiencia de una generación de Bangladesh de moverse y establecerse en Gran Bretaña
items.content_es:
Abdus Subhan y Fathema Begum. Desde Londresi Memoirs © Seema Khalique

Consciente de que las experiencias de toda una generación de británicos-Bangladeshis pronto se perderán – y motivadas celebrar la comunidad en medio de una extrema derecha – Seema Khalique construyó una pieza de historia multifacética que ahora se muestra en el verde benal de Londres

El padre de Seema Khalique llegó al Reino Unido desde Bangladesh en 1956; su madre, Gulnehar, llegó en 1973, después de la Guerra de Liberación de Bangladesh. Abdul Khalique estaba en el negocio de los restaurantes, y la familia se barroó a Croydon en los años 70 después de comprar un restaurante allí; más tarde se mudaron a Eltham, una vez más después del trabajo. Es una historia que habla de injerto y determinación,

Y así conectar con 12 individuos –muchos vinculados a su padre – Khalique pasó horas con cada uno de ellos desde 2021, escuchando sus historias, colaborando en sus retratos, y mirando a través de sus archivos. El resultado es Londoni Memoirs, un proyecto todavía en marcha apoyado por el Fondo Nacional del Patrimonio de la Lotería, que reúne historia oral, fotos de archivo, efímera, y nuevas imágenes para documentar Bangaldeshis que se estableció en Gran Bretaña en los años 50-70s. Algunos, como Khalique, se basan en Londres, otros están más acampados, aterrizando por suerte y el trabajo que estaba disponible cuando emigraron.

“Generalmente todos los participantes se mudaron donde había trabajo, así que si eso significaba ir a Birmingham, debido al comercio de fábrica allí, estaban en Birmingham”, dados Khalique. “Había una comunidad masiva en el East End debido a las fábricas allí, y eso creó oportunidades para las mujeres que trabajan desde casa – podían coser y adaptar, y estar con los niños. Todos tenían una máquina de coser. La mayoría de la gente trabajaba seis días a la semana.

Al trabajar en este nivel, las personas lograron establecerse, dados Khalique; muchos enviaron también dinero a Bangladesh, especialmente durante la guerra [en 1971]. “Muchas personas hablaron de la sensación de que habían ayudado a Bangladesh a sobrevivir”, dados. “Los miembros de la familia no se murieron de hambre porque pudieron proporcionar.”

Londoni Memoirs recoge algunas historias desgarradoras, relatos de personas que huían de aldeas quemadas – los únicos que escapan – y que regresan años más tarde, sin saber quién encontrarían vivos. Pocos de los participantes habían hablado públicamente sobre estas experiencias antes, dice Khalique, prefiriendo seguir adelante “aunque todavía llevan el trauma”. Londoni Memoirs También registra tiempos más felices, Khalique determinó no aplanar una serie de experiencias en un monotone, o muchos testimonios en una sola masa lumpen.

“Un participante provenía de una familia muy afligida, vino al Reino Unido para estudiar leyes y su padre demostrado lo financió”, señala. “Vivió en el mismo camino que los Beatles, y tenía estas historias locas sobre fiestas donde la policía persigueía a todos. Otros hablaron sobre el escaneo en Londres, como una solución a la crisis de la vivienda. Fue interesante escuchar sobre las vidas paralelas que se escuchan en ese momento, y

La sensibilidad de Khalique muestra en sus retratos, que hizo colaborativamente. Hay una fotografía dulce de su madre en su jardín, utilizando un sari verde que coincide con el fonaje de una Planta de Marrow de Bangladesh “que los Bangladesh crecen con orgullo en los meses de verano”. Khalique también ha recogido fotos de pasaporte y documentación oficial, incluyendo una fotografía increíblemente glamorosa de su madre en un pasaporte debido a expirar en 1977, y un recibo del Fondo de Socorro de Pakistán por £5, fechada en la pre-independencia 1965 [cuando £5 valía alrededor de £125 hoy]. La exposición de Khalique en Four Corners incluye videos de 10 de los participantes que hablan; ella también ha creado lo periódico todo

La ubicación de la galería es importante también porque, aunque Khalique todavía vive en el sudeste de Londres, ella quería mostrar el trabajo cerca de la comunidad británica-Bangladeshi; Four Corners está en el este de Londres, cerca de la larga ciudad de Banglatown en Whitechapel y Brick Lawed. Khalique también organizó un taller familiar en la galería, permitiendo que los niños se enteren más sobre la historia británica, Bangladesh y British-Bangladeshi, además de temas de representación; estos temas se han vuelto más importantes para ella, dados, debido a soportarcer las actitudes de extrema derecha, y porque ahora tiene hijos propios. “Crecí en un área muy multicultural, nunca me sentí racialmente diferente”, dice. “Es sólo desde que se convirtió en una

Hero, Florence, Massachusetts, 2022 © Holly Lynton.

Bristol Photo Festival’s third edition creates a palimpsest of past, present and future, explains festival director Alejandro Acín

In Castle Park, central Bristol, there is a plaque paying tribute to men from the city who joined the fight against fascism in the Spanish Civil War. “It’s always been in my mind,” says Bristol Photo Festival director Alejandro Acín. This year marks 90 years since the Spanish Civil War but, with authoritarian governments and far-right activism rising across the globe, that moment now feels uncomfortably close.

It is a reminder that the past has a way of shapeshifting into the present, and this idea reverberates through the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival. Themed Time Machine, it includes a show taking place in a cave not far from the park featuring three artists exploring the contemporary resonance of the Spanish Civil War – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia. Their work is part of a city-wide programme of exhibitions in which photography is not simply a recording of the past, but an articulation of our non-linear experience of time. Memory of what has been and speculation about the future meet in the present day. 

“Often the works that we bring explore historical events but from contemporary approaches, or vice versa, so there’s always this kind of entanglement of time that happens,” Acín notes, adding that Time Machine follows two previous editions focusing on movement (in 2024) and place (in 2021). “We can look at the three editions as almost a trilogy,” he explains.

“Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently”
– Alejandro Acín

This year a show by Goa-based artist Akshay Mahajan responds to the British Empire and Commonwealth Collection held in Bristol, drawing on Indian folklore to consider how the ghosts of colonialism still haunt the border between India and Pakistan. Italian photojournalist Giulio Di Sturco’s Anthropocosmos invites viewers into constructed spaces designed by scientists and engineers, meanwhile, to test out space conditions. His images show how humans are preparing for a potential – as yet unrealised – future beyond Earth. 

There is also an exhibition presented by Kegham Djeghalian, the son of the late Kegham Avedis Garabet Djeghalian – an Armenian-Palestinian photographer who set up Gaza’s first photographic studio. Djeghalian Senior’s images are a portal to a flourishing pre-Nakba Palestine, which stands in stark contrast to the horrifying images of destruction of recent years. Elsewhere Annie Wang’s Mother as a Creator charts the Taiwanese artist’s journey into pregnancy, through motherhood, and on to the shifting, overlapping terrain she now occupies between her maternal and creative roles.

This edition of Bristol Photo Festival is Acín’s second as director (after a stint as director of education and engagement for the first edition); alongside it he runs IC Visual Lab with co-director Ben GJ Thomas and designer/producer Safia Belhaj. ICVL is based in the middle of the city, in the one-time home of the South African Resource Centre and curator Christine Eyene is drawing on the building’s radical history for an exhibition there, featuring work by George Hallett. An award-winning South African photographer, Hallett was exiled to London in the 1970s and made portraits of anti-apartheid creatives, writers, artists and musicians.

The festival includes a busy opening week from 14 to 18 October, featuring parties, openings and a symposium; it will also include an ‘education weekend’ in its five-week run, featuring masterclasses led by photographers and industry insiders. “It’s about building relationships where participants can continue developing their work,” says Acín. 

The 2024 festival was a resounding success. Amak Mahmoodian’s exhibition in it, One Hundred and Twenty Minutes, went on to earn a Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize nomination, while some 40 per cent of those who went to the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery during its run were visiting the institution for the first time. “We had visitors from every postcode in Bristol, so on a local level we had pretty good engagement,” says Acín.

However, since then much has changed in Bristol (and beyond), with arts organisations facing a tougher funding landscape than ever. Bristol Photo Festival consists of curated exhibitions – rather than depending on an open call – which provides an income for some; this puts more financial pressure on the festival, and more onus on partnership. The closure of the Royal Photographic Society’s gallery has also had an impact, as it was previously a key venue – although some new spaces have come on board.

The festival, along with the wider photography community, is also still mourning the loss of Martin Parr in December 2025, a long-term Bristol resident and keen advocate of the programme. “It was very sad,” says Acín. “Martin was part of the board and he was always helpful with contacts, interested and supportive of the festival.” The festival maintains close ties with the Martin Parr Foundation, whose group exhibition Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic will be on show during its run; the popular Books on Photography will also return to MPF on 17 and 18 October.

Acín is open about the difficulties, believing it is important for organisations to speak up about the impact of massive cuts to public arts in the UK, and the loss of access to EU funding post-Brexit. “It’s a reality that’s very palpable, very tangible,” he says. “Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently.”

Bristol Photo Festival takes place from 14 October–15 November 2026. BOP is the weekend of 17–18 October 2026.

items.title_es: Bristol Photo Festival 2026 entra en la máquina del tiempo
items.content_es:
Hero, Florence, Massachusetts2022 © Holly Lynton.

La tercera edición de Bristol Photo Festival crea un palimpsesto del pasado, presente y futuro, explica el director del festival Alejandro Acín

En Castle Park, el centro de Bristol, hay una placa que rinde homenaje a los hombres de la ciudad que se unieron a la lucha contra el fascismo en la Guerra Civil Española. “Siempre ha estado en mi mente”, Alejandro Acín, director del Festival de Fotografía de Bristol. Este año se celebra 90 años desde la Guerra Civil española, pero con gobiernos autoritarios y activismo de extrema derecha que se elevan por todo el mundo, ese momento se siente cerca.

Es un recordatorio de que el pasado tiene una forma de modelar en el presente, y esta idea reverbera a través del Festival Fotográfico de Bristol 2026. Máquina del tiempo, incluye un espectáculo que se realiza en una cueva no muy lejos del parque con tres artistas que exploran la resonancia contemporánea de la Guerra Civil Española – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón y Natasha Christia. Su trabajo forma parte de un programa de exposiciones en toda la ciudad en el que la fotografía no es simplemente una grabación del pasado, sino una articulación de nuestra experiencia no lineal del tiempo. Memoria de lo que ha sido y especulación sobre el día de futuro.

“A menudo las obras que traemos exploran eventos históricos pero desde enfoques contemporáneos, o viceversa, así que siempre hay este tipo de enredo del tiempo que sucede”, señala Acín, agregando que Máquina del tiempo sigue dos ediciones anteriores centradas en el movimiento (en 2024) y el lugar (en 2021). “Podemos ver las tres ediciones como casi una trilogía”, explica.

“La cultura de este año es más política que nunca. Luchamos para mantener espacios que permitan a la gente pensar, hablar y mirar el mundo de manera diferente”
– Alejandro Acín

Este año un espectáculo del artista radicado en Goa Akshay Mahajan responde al Imperio Británico y la Colección Commonwealth celebrada en Bristol, aprovechando el folclore indio para considerar cómo los fantasmas del colonialismo todavía persiguen la frontera entre India y Pakistán. Antropocosmos invita a los espectadores a espacios construidos diseñados por científicos e ingenieros, mientras tanto, a probar las condiciones espaciales. Sus imágenes muestran cómo los humanos se están preparando para un futuro potencial – aún no realizado– más allá de la Tierra.

También hay una exposición presentada por Kegham Djeghalian, el hijo del fallecido Kegham Avedis Garabet Djeghalian – un fotógrafo armenio-palestino que creó el primer estudio fotográfico de Gaza. Las imágenes de Djeghalian Senior son un portal para una próspera Palestina pre-Nakba, que contrasta con las horribles imágenes de destrucción de los últimos años. Madre como Creador traza el viaje de la artista taiwanesa al embarazo, a través de la maternidad, y en el terreno cambiante y superpuesto que ocupa ahora entre sus roles materno-creativos.

Esta edición de Bristol Photo Festival es la segunda como directora de Acín (después de ser directora de educación y compromiso para la primera edición); junto con ella dirige IC Visual Lab con el codirector Ben GJ Thomas y el diseñador/productor Safia Belhaj. ICVL se basa en el centro de la ciudad, en la casa única del South African Resource Centre y la curadora Christine Eyene está dibujando en la historia radical del edificio

El festival incluye una semana de apertura ocupada del 14 al 18 de octubre, con fiestas, aperturas y un simposio; también ahorrar un “fin de semana educativa” en su carrera de cinco semanas, con masterclasses liderados por fotógrafos e internadores de la industria. “Es sobre la construcción de relaciones donde los participantes pueden continuar desarrollando su trabajo”, dice Acín.

El festival 2024 fue un éxito resonante. Exposición de Amak Mahmoodian en él, Un centenar y veinte minutos, siguió ganando una nominación del Premio Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation, mientras que alrededor del 40% de los que fueron al Museo de Bristol y a la Galería de Arte durante su carrera estuvieron visitando la institución por primera vez. “Tuvimos visitantes de cada código postal en Bristol, así que a nivel local tuvimos bastante buen compromiso”, dice Acín.

Sin embargo, desde entonces mucho ha cambiado espacios en Bristol (y más allá), con organizaciones de arte frente a un paisaje de financiación más difícil que nunca. Bristol Photo Festival consiste en exposiciones curadas – en lugar de dependencia de una llamada abierta – que proporciona un ingreso para algunos; esto pone más presión financiera en el festival, y más onus en la asociación. El cierre de la galería de la Royal Photographic Society también ha tenido un impacto, ya que era anteriormente un lugar clave –

El festival, junto con la comunidad de fotografía más amplia, sigue lamentando la pérdida de Martin Parr en diciembre de 2025, residente de Bristol a largo plazo y entusiasta defensor del programa. “Fue muy triste”, dice Acín. “Martin fue parte del consejo y siempre fue útil con los contactos, interesado y solidario del festival”. El festival mantiene estrechos vínculos con la Fundación Martin Parr, cuya exposición colectiva Cuentos oscuros: Fotografía documental británica y gótico estará en exhibición durante su carrera; los populares Libros sobre Fotografía también volverán a MPF los días 17 y 18 de octubre.

Acín está abierto sobre las dificultades, creyendo que es importante que las organizaciones hablann sobre el impacto de los recortes masivos a las artes públicas en el Reino Unido, y la pérdida de acceso a la financiación de la UE post-Brexit. “Es una realidad muy palpable, muy tangible”, dados. “La cultura de este año es más política que nunca. Estamos luchando para mantener espacios que permitan a la gente pensar, hablar y mirar el mundo de manera diferente”.

Bristol Photo Festival tiene lugar del 14 de octubre al 15 de noviembre de 2026. BOP es el fin de semana del 17 al 18 de octubre de 2026.

items.title: Restoring the fractured archive: SWANA collective memory at BredaPhoto Festival
items.excerpt: © Majd Arandas Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North
items.content:
© Majd Arandas

Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives

For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material.

Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation. 

This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through. Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context.

“This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed

Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging.

“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed.

“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”

Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep, presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework. 

Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary. 

Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us.

“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].” 

Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years. She refuses to use folklore as mere nostalgia, but positions it as a perpetual tool of survival, demonstrating its inherent political utility. Her lens is patient and meditative, a direct rejection of the high-velocity aesthetic of breaking news stories disseminated in a 24-hour cycle; instead it asserts an invisible, unbreakable network of spatial permanence.

“For me, it’s a work of deliberate digging, of continuous searching  – instead of considering the past as framed and fixed,” she says. “Because this is very dangerous, particularly in the context of Palestine. Once the past is turned into mere symbols, there is a risk of not being able to breathe anymore. It becomes empty. And for me, the collective memory is all about the embodied practices, knowledge, our rituals and the visceral connection to our land  – whether in joy or in loss, in a funeral for a martyr that turns into celebration.” 

Abed insists on the preservation of memories, by transforming them and keeping them connected to the present. “To simply lean on the past in this utopian way, with distance, there is no resistance for that in me,” she says. “This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination, that gives us both the hope and the means to rehearse liberation. Because there is no future other than liberation.” 

While Abed maps the deep roots of connection to the land, Fouad Hallak’s A Mind in the Past, Eyes on Tomorrow addresses the fractured geometries of exile and return. Born in Syria, Hallak fled the country on a migrant vessel to claim asylum in the Netherlands; his work shifts away from diasporic trauma towards an internalised psychogeography. His recent documentation tracks his return to his homeland, in transition following the fall of Assad, capturing the fragile space between historical devastation and actualised hope.

“After the fall of the Assad regime, I noticed that people often looked at what happened in two different ways – some stories were bright, and others were painful,” Hallak reflects. “But these feelings can exist at the same time. When I went back, I was not an outsider. I was part of the story. I see this in the photograph of Khaled, who protested and fought against the regime. He carries his history with him and still moves forward… Before, this possibility did not exist. Now it does. For me, that is hope.”

Fascinated by old studio portraiture, and saddened by its disappearance due to war, Hallak created a temporary mobile setup in the streets of Damascus. Inviting residents to have their portraits taken, he constructed a new archive of Syrian presence with his series, Studio Damascus. 

“When survival becomes part of everyday life, the simple act of having a portrait taken becomes difficult,” he says. “I believe that having a portrait taken with your family can be a sign of stability. When I direct people in front of the camera, the connection creates a moment in which they can step away from their instability. Studio Damascus explores reunion, memory, belonging, and the human need for stability.”

Hallak refuses to flatten the reality of a community navigating a shattered state. “After all these years, I still feel there is a desire to make these realities easier to understand,” he concludes. “I don’t think the problem is misunderstanding. This is what I search for in my practice – a language that comes from human feeling. Something emotional, intimate, and perhaps even spiritual.”

Meanwhile photographer and filmmaker Fatima Joumaa turns the counter-archive towards the structural realities of South Lebanon (Al-Janoub) and Beirut’s southern suburbs (Dahiyeh). In her intimate project From My Mother’s Novel: Returning to South Lebanon, she weaves images through her mother Layla’s old notes and sketches, creating a meditation on grief, memory, and women as keepers of history. Joumaa combines analogue photography, poetic video essays, and first-hand local testimonies to directly challenge the usual media representations of war.

Whenever life in Lebanon is ruptured – and there have been many compounding crises over the past seven years alone, long before Israel’s current genocidal assault and occupation of the South – global image-makers flood the streets, capturing the immediate violence and debris, the grief and rage, before equally swiftly departing. This high-velocity reportage leaves what Joumaa calls an “after-image” in its wake, a concept she has developed into a series for independent Lebanese magazine The Public Source.

Shifting her gaze toward the quiet, slow-burning aftermath and complex interiorities that unfold after the intrusive cameras leave, she fights the persistent clichés that reduce entire neighbourhoods and their inhabitants to passive sites of devastation. “I was always aware of how much the image is treated as an extractable resource, whether moving or still,” she says. “And often, when international media or institutions approach us, they want the image because it carries a kind of authenticity – but they want to decide what that authenticity is allowed to contain.

“I have been asked to remove flags, portraits of martyrs, political signs, or anything that might make the image appear too political to them, as if there’s anything that isn’t political,” she continues. “And I refuse to portray my people only as victims.”

Joumaa argues these signifiers are at the core of this landscape, not mere additions to it – and that removing them does not render the image more neutral. Quite the opposite. “It produces another complete image, one that is more comfortable for the institution,” she says. “To them, it simply checks a box of exclusivity [paying lip-service to local perspectives] rather than talking about what is fundamentally happening.”

For Joumaa, the Israeli assault on South Lebanon, and its systematic violent occupation and genocidal destruction of almost all of the land in the region, is an everyday reality. She could not return to her village in Janoub to bury her grandmother, as is the reality for many families in South Lebanon. But by integrating first-person local testimonies into her video essays, she ensures that the voices of the community dictate the narrative arc of the work; the record of survival is written in the smallest, most intimate – most often overlooked – pockets of human existence.

Centring the camera on home-bound networks of care, Joumaa suggests that sovereignty is maintained through everyday acts of defiance, not on a grand geopolitical stage. And her insistence on documenting the unseen, foundational rhythms of community forms a natural bridge to Kuwaiti photographer and researcher Huda Abdulmughni, whose work focuses on the ancestral landscape.

Where Joumaa’s lens operates as an almost forensic instrument within the targeted spaces of her land and people, Abdulmughni focuses on a different kind of survival – one grounded in ecological harmony and collective memory.  Abdulmughni’s Nowruz Sayadeen documents the annual fisherman’s New Year on the Iranian island of Qeshm, for example, in which the village’s primary source of income is paused, out of respect for nature’s seasonal bounty. Using both analogue and digital media, Abdulmughni captures the highly-stylised, almost mythical cast of characters populating the shores, including the iconic shushis – figures adorned with white face paint and palm leaves.

But rather than presenting the figures as exotic subjects, performing in costume once a year, Abdulmughni captures a world that relies on ancestral knowledge of the seas. Depicting traditions passed down through the generations, outside the strict categories preferred by Western ethnography, Abdulmughni’s work demonstrates that regional sovereignty is preserved through seasonal rhythms and ancestral ecological care. But her work also shows that this is also a world increasingly impacted by climate change due to geopolitical conflict, in which the community’s harmony with the earth may be devastated. 

The biennial takes a devastating turn to remind us of the stakes raised when gentle rhythms are severed by colonial violence, including a posthumous show by Majd Arandas, A Memorial in Fragments. Arandas’ work brings the viewer face-to-face with the realities of active elimination; born in Gaza in 1994, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike near his home in Deir al-Balah on 01 November 2023. Arandas had long ago been forced to sell his professional camera to survive the Israeli blockade, but continued to document with his mobile phone, and his archive has been retrieved and preserved by his brother. 

Somji wanted to honour Arandas’ work and life, but also show the networks of solidarity that surrounded him, and now surround his archive. “Whether it’s a beautiful exchange between Majd and a friend about the plants in his beloved grandmother’s garden, or a photographer friend exchanging cat photos with him, it shows how communities find ways to bond together, and provide solace, despite everything that’s against them, despite the challenges of neoliberal worlds and neo-colonialist regimes,” Somji says. 

Arandas’ surviving images testify to what it means to create an archive when your existence is being contested in real-time. But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. His work refuses to let his people be remembered solely by their erasure, insisting instead on the profound beauty and unyielding right to exist that defined their daily survival.

These exhibitions help make Our Songs Came Through a significant biennale; they also surface the often behind-the-scenes negotiations required to present these images within a Western framework. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition.

Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making.

Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives. They remind us that history is not merely written by the victors, even those who wield a camera; it is unobtrusively and persistently preserved in the songs that survive, the rituals that map, and the communities which refuse to be forgotten. The fractured archive is reimagined as a site of radical agency, resistance, and complexity, and it honours the nuances of daily human survival. 

BredaPhoto Festival 2026, Our Songs Came Through, is open until 25 October https://bredaphoto.nl

items.title: Thinking through technology
items.excerpt: Requiem for an Exit, 2025 © Kvam Oldereid A new exhibition and the THEA space in Groningen, Netherlands, use art to think through technology and human experience, explains curator and director Roosje Klap Last year the Nooderlicht Biennale was themed Machine Entanglements and
items.content:
Requiem for an Exit, 2025 © Kvam Oldereid

A new exhibition and the THEA space in Groningen, Netherlands, use art to think through technology and human experience, explains curator and director Roosje Klap

Last year the Nooderlicht Biennale was themed Machine Entanglements and, including exhibitions by 75 artists across the northern Dutch city of Groningen, explored “how we now live, eat, sleep, dream and even date through technology,” says Roosje Klap, director of Nooderlicht, the platform for photography and lens-based media. The shows in one venue, THEA, focused on extraction – the “ugly monster” which makes technology, as Klap puts it – and, working in the building, she was called to reception one day. “There was this guy, maybe about 55, and he was very emotional because he had seen all this for the first time,” she explains. 

“He had known about it, but this was the first time he had really seen it. That was very important for me, very touching, but then he asked, ‘Is there any hope? Because I don’t see any hope, only sadness and terrible feelings’. And that’s when I started to wonder, what’s the way out? There must be a way out, how can we escape, or what’s the antidote?” That insight led to the latest exhibition at THEA, Thinking Hands, which explores how embodied knowledge endures in our ever-more technological age.

Curated by Klap with Musoke Nalwoga, Thinking Hands includes both still and moving work, and finds quirky, thought-provoking twists on the theme. There’s Paul Kooiker’s series Talking Hands, for example, a playful look at body language, and there’s Martina Bacigalupo’s found series Gulu Real Art Studio – a series of studio portraits, in which the heads had been clipped out of the image to make passport photos. Removing the face as a point of focus, Gulu Real Art Studio throws the attention on the sitters’ hands and postures, and what they express. 

Andi Gáldi Vinkó’s Sorry I Gave Birth I Disappeared But Now I’m Back explores the deeply embodied experience of early motherhood, a time in which the baby is technically separate but is often ‘joined at the hip’; Martha Rosler’s Semiotics of the Kitchen, from the generation before Gáldi Vinkó, rethinks cookery skills as enforced, internalised physical socialisation. Laure Prouvost’s Taking Care (Love letter to a fellow art work) depicts the artist as art handler, talking to a viewer as if he or she is a painting or object; Requiem for an Exit by Kvam/Oldereid shows an eerie armless robot, whose disembodied projected face and AI-generated voice speak of genocide and human displacement. 

“All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human.” Roosje Klap

Klap takes me on a virtual tour, walking me through the space via her laptop; we’re 300 miles apart but she’s warm and funny, cracking jokes through cyberspace. “All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human,” she smiles, turning the laptop back to herself and reflecting on how instinctively we now use technology. And photography, of course, is part of that process. 

“The apparatus is part of the body, and the decision to make that photo – yes or no – is also an embodied decision,” Klap muses. “I think it is really a mind/body-correlative decision, and I feel that’s very much at the basis of what’s at stake now [as technology expands], because we are taking ourselves out of that whole system.” 

And her lively engagement with technology is important because, as well as being director of Noorderlicht, Klap is now Cultural Development Lead at Niemeyer. The Niemeyer is a former tobacco factory now being developed into a public culture and tech hub and THEA has some 8000 square metres of space in it, spread over three floors; THEA is backed by the Mondriaan Fund and support from the City of Groningen, and its mission is to explore the impact of technology via art and culture. The project is a two-year startup so far but, says Klap, she’s “here to stay”, and she is co-developing THEA with Rosa Wevers, an independent curator and senior researcher in Art & Technology at Hanze University.

THEA is also developing alongside the other initiatives at the Niemeyer, which include projects such as the AI Factory; part of an EU-backed network of projects using AI to help research healthcare and agriculture, the AI Factory aims to rethink the technology with privacy, security, and digital sovereignty in mind. “The AI Factories are being put into place as alternatives to big tech, so they are interesting and important,” says Klap. “But that’s where THEA is important too.

“That work is all happening in computers; we can help make it more visible. We can also be a critical little sister to Big Brother and the tech bros. THEA and the tech companies [which are moving into Niemeyer] are an integral part of each other.” 

In fact THEA is named after a rebellious female figure; Theodora Niemeyer was the daughter of tobacco company founder Theodorus Niemeyer but, rather than pursuing the bourgeois life into which she was born in 1912, went to the Hague and became a painter. She used her inheritance to create an art fund. “I wanted to honour her, and so the programme is divided into three areas,” says Klap. “It’s a combination of making, doing and talking about art, so there’s art and technology; care and technology, which includes symposia and critical thinking; and make and technology, which for example includes hackerspace.”

THEA will be a key venue for the Noorderlicht Biennale next summer, which will be themed PLAY; the theme suggests latitude to explore computer games and gaming culture, and while Klap – who will be artistic lead – is keen to embrace these forms, she’s also thinking less literally. She wants to include Debi Cornwall’s Necessary Fictions / Model Citizens, for example, which explore Hollywood film tropes and their impact on people’s perceptions, the stereotypes which inform our reactions without us being consciously aware of them. 

As before the biennale will be spread over six or seven locations across Groningen, both the city and the wider province; Klap was born in Amsterdam and studied in the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, but moved to Groningen two years ago and says it’s a traditionally radical city. “Groningen is known as the red heart of the Netherlands,” says Klap, who I interviewed shortly before far right clashes in The Hague. “Something I find really great here is that I don’t have to explain to politicians that culture is important for society.”

Thinking Hands is on show at THEA, Groningen until 01 November noorderlicht.com/en/whats-on/thinking-hands

items.excerpt: Aperture’s new home at 380 Columbus Avenue, New York. Image courtesy Aperture As Aperture moves to the Upper West Side, and puts a renewed focus on reaching out, executive director Sarah Meister reflects on its ‘tentacular’ past and future Nothing says “killing it” like
items.content:
Aperture’s new home at 380 Columbus Avenue, New York. Image courtesy Aperture

As Aperture moves to the Upper West Side, and puts a renewed focus on reaching out, executive director Sarah Meister reflects on its ‘tentacular’ past and future

Nothing says “killing it” like buying real estate in an outlandishly expensive culture-rich metropolitan hub. Aperture, the nonprofit publisher of sleek photobooks and the esteemed magazine, has done just that, purchasing and settling in a new permanent home that’s just opened to the public.

The 74-year-old organisation now occupies two floors of a New York City building dating back to 1886, refurbished by architecture practice Levenbetts (which was also behind the Queens Museum and five New York Public Libraries). “Because it was a residential building, it has an intimacy to it,” says Aperture’s executive director Sarah Meister, and the ground-floor entrance boasts street-level visibility to appeal more widely to passers-by, not just to photography devotees. (“Serious photographers will find you on the fourth floor of a side street in Chelsea,” Meister notes.)

Aperture’s new home is on the Upper West Side, which might seem unexpected given the centripetal force of New York’s downtown art scene. But “trendy arts neighbourhoods… move with fashion,” Meister reasons. By contrast, Aperture’s new neighbours are institutions such as the American Museum of Natural History and the New York Historical, and Central Park is just a stone’s throw away. They – and it – aren’t going anywhere. 

Moreover, the singularity of the real estate gives it cachet. Meister points out that “it has 140-year-old load-bearing masonry, and it just has a great feel to it”, and Aperture was able to make the purchase through funding from private individuals such as Judy Glickman Lauder and Jon Stryker, as well as grants from New York State Council on the Arts and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs.

“It’s not a white box, and it never will be.” Sarah Meister

Inside the entrance – and past a Majestic Photobooth – the bookstore features Aperture’s output, which includes four issues of the magazine plus 12 books per year, and a backlist which unfurls as far back as the mid-1960s. It also features a pop-up collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York City’s de facto photobook purveyor; founder David Strettell will present a savvy selection of titles to sit alongside Aperture’s publications, and some of his knowledgeable staff will move uptown. “It’s just a smarter way of being,” Meister says, “rather than us trying to do what they do, because they do it so well.”

Aperture will host book launches in the shop, including for a new monograph by Elle Pérez, and for the Catherine Opie edition of The Photography Workshop Series; the Aperture PhotoBook Club will also create an opportunity for follow-up discussions. The shop features some lighthearted collaborations on merch too – there are Vik Muniz printed umbrellas, for example, and placemats printed with images from Stephen Shore’s American Surfaces. There are also baseball caps and tote bags, branded with the Aperture logo.

“There’ll be a handful of things in the store in collaboration with artists or people whose design sensibility we really respect,” Meister enthuses. “So we hope you come in for the books and the magazine, but there will be other fun things to buy too.”

The building’s two levels – one is half below street-level, and one is half above – give visitors views into key work areas, providing a behind-the-scenes peek into Aperture’s activities. The magazine team, the production team, and the book team are visibly present. “You can see in, and we’re happy about that. I think it’s going to give us a new understanding of our audience,” Meister says. Staff are encouraged to sit at a table in the bookstore, and listen and talk to people walking by. 

The building also features a dedicated gallery space and the inaugural exhibition, which was curated by Meister, spotlights photographers who have been integral to depicting New York City, including Diane Arbus, Tina Barney, Dawoud Bey, Awol Erizku, Lee Friedlander, Nan Goldin, Deana Lawson, and Carrie Mae Weems. There’s a print loaned from the Robert Frank Foundation; some artists made new 8x10s.

Temporary exhibitions will generally be on view in the space for six to eight week stretches, though Meister says “we don’t want to become too rigid”. That ethos will run through the shows too, with most works leant on a picture rail on a shelf, rather than hung, leaving the original exposed brick undisturbed. “That lack of preciousness is very intentional,” Meister explains. “A little bit of informality feels like a nice thing. Our wall text is going to be printed on an 11×17 sheet with magnets on a beautiful little metal panel: very simple.” 

In the longer term, Aperture is working with artists to develop different configurations for the space, allowing each individual to use it in their own way. “It’s not a white box, and it never will be,” Meister affirms, adding that Alex Webb, Dionne Lee, and Angélica Dass will be showing there in future. 

Aperture will run public events in the gallery, with a series of conversations “between pairs of people who either know one another or one another’s work well”. Stephen Shore and Lucy Gallun, curator in the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art, will speak together on 03 October, for example, then Gillian Laub and Jil Weinstock, director of Baxter St, on 14 October; Coreen Simpson and Rujeko Hockley, curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, will be in conversation on 21 October. Aperture will also continue to organise large-scale touring exhibitions.

Aperture also offers an educational program, with online curricula offered free of charge to public school teachers and kids. As Meister says: “Somebody once described Aperture as tentacular, which I love – not just because it rhymes with spectacular! It captures the breadth of what we do.”

Aperture, 380 Columbus Avenue, New York, NY 10024 aperture.org

items.title: Re-finding Fran – celebrating Francesca Odell’s overlooked documentary work
items.excerpt: After the night feed. Rhydian, Michelle and Rachael – Garden village, Gilfach Goch – December 1985 © Francesca Odell/Ffotogallery. On show for the first time in 30 years, Francesca Odell’s warm, intimate images finally get their due “My pictures reflect my i
items.content:
After the night feed. Rhydian, Michelle and Rachael – Garden village, Gilfach Goch – December 1985 © Francesca Odell/Ffotogallery.

On show for the first time in 30 years, Francesca Odell’s warm, intimate images finally get their due

“My pictures reflect my interest in people and the very different ways we have of coping with and enjoying life,” wrote Francesca Odell. “I try to convey the essential humanity we share as individuals, despite sometimes very adverse situations, believing that through knowledge and understanding, we can come to a more tolerant attitude towards each other and, perhaps ultimately, change for the better.”

Opening on 04 October at The Turner House as part of Ffoto Cymru, Francesca Odell: Coping With and Enjoying Life is a posthumous show, and the first on Odell’s work in 30 years. Curated by Sam McGuire and Chloe Davies, it focuses on Odell’s commissions for the Valleys Project, which McGuire discovered while researching for her PhD on the project in the gallery’s archive. “What’s so great about Odell’s work is the way I believe she approached her practice,” says McGuire. 

“I don’t see her images as representations of the socio-economic context of that period. The works are embedded in that political moment, and they offer some form of commentary… but I see her works as photographs of people.”

Fran, to those who knew her, was born in 1951 and passed away in 2022; she discovered her talent for photography late and almost incidentally, and took up her place on the famous Diploma in Documentary Photography at Newport College of Art in 1984, after becoming a single parent. Odell completed the course and went on to win prestigious commissions, before ending up leaving professional photography to become an archivist at the National Portrait Gallery. 

“I try to convey the essential humanity we share as individuals, despite sometimes very adverse situations.” Francesca Odell

‘Doc Phot’ was set up by Magnum’s David Hurn, who designed the course around getting people into work in the photographic industry, and former students remember it as being both diverse and elite. Photographers such as Martin Parr and Josef Koudelka would drop by, and the small group of students ranged from Oxbridge graduates to those from ‘back to work’ programmes. Chosen for their ideas over their images, the lucky few would embark on an intensive two-year course that required them to shoot and print work daily. Leaving her three daughters with their father, Odell moved alone to Newport and threw herself into it.

“She had an intense interest in people and their lives and their livelihoods,” says Naomi Fulford, one of Odell’s children. “She would be incredibly empathetic, and just showed a real interest in what people did – whether it was on a grander scale or on the most simplistic level. She was able to bring people into her sphere and to engage with them at a really intimate level.”

Naomi and her sisters, Eleanor Thompson and Lorelei Mariner, were all under ten when this new creative calling consumed their mother; too young to understand it then, they are now thrilled her work is being recognised. They feature regularly in Odell’s archive, as she photographed them each time she returned to Sandy Lane – an alternative community in the Gower where she lived with her daughters before moving to Newport. She went back after Newport, and again after her retiring from the NPG. and her photographs of Sandy Lane show the people who had chosen a radical lifestyle at a time of great societal change.

Daniel Meadows, who taught on the Doc Phot course, remembers Odell as a talented, committed course-member, and a lovely person who he stayed in touch with. “There were very few postgraduate courses in the practice of photography [at that time], and absolutely none in documentary photography [except Newport]. It attracted an enormous range of different kinds of people to it.” 

“She was always very intense, once you got into looking at the work. She was always very keen to make better pictures, but she would always interrogate your solutions to how she should go about stuff, she would challenge you…in a very polite way. So a good student, because that’s the kind of student you want.”

Meadows recalls Odell’s projects on local female bodybuilders and a community at the local Turkish baths, which he hadn’t realised existed. Odell sought out stories that interested her, mostly around women, and got to know her subjects, creating a bond of trust that is palpable in the warmth and intimacy of her images. Her most famous work is the series of commissions she was awarded as part of the Valleys project organised through Ffotogallery, which had a remit to capture “social, industrial and topographic change” in the South Wales valleys at that time. 

There was a close connection between the gallery, the Doc Phot course and the project, mostly due to their proximity, but the commission was wide-ranging and included photographers such as David Bailey and Ron McCormick; starting in 1984, it yielded an archive of some 450 images, shot by ten image-makers. Odell’s work stands out for its tenderness, and its positive focus in what was a challenging time for many; her connections with the people she photographed are evident, and struck McGuire when she found the work.

“There is an image called After the Night Feed that I was just completely enamoured with,” she recalls. “I’m a parent and the image captures such a recognisable feeling. There’s something incredibly emotive about it, and the idea that a photographer had access to that moment was fascinating to me. I just set about a kind of exploration, ‘Who was she? How did she get this access? How did she earn the trust of these subjects?’ And then to find out that there is nothing written about her…” 

The lack of information about Odell, the fact that nothing of her existed online except a staff photo from the NPG, led McGuire to focus on Odell in her PhD, research which precipitated the Turner House show. “The sadness – but also the joy – of the exhibition is that it is able to give this snapshot of two-and-a-half years of a photographer’s life,” she muses. “All of the projects [on show] are made in that period, and actually, it’s probably a shorter period even than that. The images are all made from 1984 to 1985.”

Paul Reas – who also shot on the Valleys project, and was a technician on the Doc Phot course while Odell was studying – echoes these words. He remembers Odell’s talent, and how nice she was, and how, as a single parent working in a fast-changing industry, she had to choose stability over an unpredictable freelance photography career. He wishes she could have lived to see the exhibition, describing it as “a bittersweet moment”. 

Francesca Odell: Coping With and Enjoying Life is a snapshot of what might in other circumstances have been a great career; it also testifies to a life well-lived. Odell is remembered with great affection by her family and friends, and the warmth and human connection in her images live on.

Francesca Odell: Coping With and Enjoying Life – Photographs from South Wales 1983-1985 at The Turner House runs from 4 October to 8 November 2026. Ffoto Cymru runs at venues across Wales 02 October to 31 October, 2026 under theme There’s More to Life https://turnerhouse.wales/  https://www.ffotogallery.org/ffoto-cymru-2026-about
